# Upbound Group (UPBD) — Forensic Dossier

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from six consecutive earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

Upbound Group is the renamed parent of Rent-A-Center. It runs three businesses aimed at consumers who sit outside the traditional credit system: Rent-A-Center (the legacy rent-to-own store chain), Acima (a virtual lease-to-own platform embedded at the checkout of roughly 35,000-plus merchant locations), and Brigit (a subscription financial-wellness and small-dollar-liquidity app, acquired January 2025). This is, at its core, a subprime consumer-credit business dressed in fintech language.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has shifted meaningfully across these six quarters, and not entirely by choice.

**The opening note (Q1 2025) was triumphant and valedictory.** Mitch Fadel, on his "30th and final earnings call," framed Upbound as "stronger today than it's ever been," with Acima "on a tear since late 2023" booking record revenue while *improving* charge-offs. The pitch was a virtuous flywheel: trade-down demand (shoppers stepping down from prime credit) feeding Acima, a fast-growing Brigit, and a Rent-A-Center deliberately shrunk for quality.

**By mid-2025 the story tightened around discipline.** New CEO Fahmi Karam (promoted from CFO in June 2025) leaned on "protecting our balance sheet with prudent risk management" and deleveraging toward "2x leverage towards the end of next year." Growth was still the headline, but the supporting beam was credit caution.

**Q3 2025 was the crack in the narrative.** Karam had to "address the lower margin and higher loss performance at Acima" — a cohort of Q2 leases "with elevated early defaults, mainly to new customers in our e-commerce channels." The flywheel claim quietly inverted: trade-down was now a hoped-for offset to a deteriorating consumer, not a guaranteed tailwind. Management pivoted to "maybe… we will be overtightened" — choosing lower growth to defend losses.

**Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 completed the pivot to a self-help, "transformation" story.** The language is now dominated by deleveraging (2.9x → 2.6x), "data, advanced analytics and AI," and a parade of new C-suite hires (CFO Hal Khouri ex-goeasy, a Chief Growth Officer, a Chief Technology Officer). Acima GMV (gross merchandise value, the dollar value of goods leased) actually *fell year-over-year* in Q1 2026 — the first decline in the window — as tightening bit. The growth driver that powered the 2025 story has been deliberately throttled.

**Net:** the arc moved from "best-ever growth company" to "disciplined operator deleveraging through a choppy subprime cycle, hoping the AI/digital initiatives compound later." Growth was the headline in Q1 2025; balance-sheet repair is the headline now.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Acima has been on a tear… highest ever quarterly revenue" (Q1 2025); GMV +9% → +16% → +11% across 2025 | Consolidated revenue +8.7% YoY to $4.70B (FY2025); TTM revenue ~$4.5–4.7B. Real, but driven by Acima + ~two-thirds of a year of Brigit, not the whole company | **Matches — partially.** Acima growth was real; consolidated growth is more pedestrian and has now reversed, with Acima GMV turning negative in Q1 2026 |
| "Stronger today than it's ever been" (Q1 2025) | Net income $73M (FY2025) vs $123M (FY2024) — down ~41%; EPS $1.25 vs $2.21, **−43% YoY**; ROIC just 4.6% | **Diverges sharply.** Earnings nearly halved in the very year management called the company its strongest ever |
| Charge-offs improving / "within target range" | Acima charge-offs spiked to ~10% by Q4 2025 before recovering to ~8.8% in Q1 2026; net margin a razor-thin 1.6% | **Mixed.** The Q3-Q4 2025 deterioration was real and initially downplayed; the Q1 2026 recovery is genuine but recent |
| Deleveraging toward 2x | Net debt $1.63B (balance sheet, Mar 2026); leverage ~2.6x, down from 2.9x at year-end 2025 | **Matches.** The most credible part of the story — cash generation is real |
| Free cash flow strength ("nearly 4x larger" Q1 2025) | TTM FCF $333M; price-to-FCF ~5x; FY FCF 3-yr CAGR −16.3% (lumpy) | **Matches on level, not trend.** Current FCF is robust and cheap; the multi-year trend is choppy, not compounding |

The forensic tension is plain: management's prose ran hottest (Q1 2025 "best ever") in the exact year EPS fell 43% and net margin collapsed to 1.6%. The numbers say "cheap, cash-generative, but low-quality and cyclically pressured," not "best-ever."

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Declining, then stabilizing defensively.**

- **Q1 2025 (Rising/peak):** "stronger than it's ever been," "on a tear," offensive, growth-forward.
- **Q2 2025 (Stable):** "discipline in protecting our balance sheet" — first real defensive tilt; growth still claimed.
- **Q3 2025 (Declining):** forced to "address the lower margin and higher loss performance," "maybe… we will be overtightened" — clearly on the back foot.
- **Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 (Defensive-stable):** heavy reliance on "transformation," "data… AI," and leadership additions. The vocabulary shifted decisively from offense (growth, share gains) to defense (efficiency, cost optimization, prudence, "challenging operating environment"). Guidance is reaffirmed, not raised.

The shift from "trade-down is a tailwind" to "the macro is… pressuring our consumers' collective confidence" (Q3 2025) is the clearest tell.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-to-High on hitting numbers, with a sandbagging caveat.** The screener shows a 7-for-7 quarterly earnings-beat rate, and management consistently "exceeded the midpoint or high end" of guided ranges (Q1, Q2 2025). That is a real, repeatable pattern — and it cuts both ways: a 100% beat rate over seven quarters suggests deliberately conservative guideposts, so beats should be treated as expected rather than as upside surprises.

The one credibility ding: Acima's Q2-Q3 2025 loss spike was *not* foreshadowed in the Q1 2025 confidence and required mid-year mitigation. They caught it and fixed it (Q1 2026 charge-offs improved 130 bps sequentially), but they did not see it coming early. Reliability on the controllable (cost, deleveraging, guidance ranges) is High; foresight on credit vintages is Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Credit quality at Acima** — the dominant recurring question (Kyle Joseph, Bobby Griffin, Hoang Nguyen, multiple quarters). The "we're conservative / overtightened" answer was tested and partially vindicated, but the Q2-Q3 vintage problem proves analysts were right to push.
- **Legal accruals** — John Rowan (Q2 2025) pressed on a $32M accrual tied to a multi-state attorneys-general matter and the McBurnie case (a legacy Acceptance Now liability). Management framed settlements as "progress," but this is an open, multi-year overhang on a subprime lender.
- **The path back to growth in 2026** — analysts repeatedly asked whether GMV reacceleration depends on credit loosening. Management leaned on merchant-count additions and a new furniture-checkout deal, not on the consumer healing — an admission the cycle is a headwind they cannot control.
- **Brigit competition** — analysts flagged competitors "jumping along and developing or acquiring similar products." The differentiation answer was thin.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 EPS fell 43% in FY2025 (the year management called it "best ever"); net margin is just 1.6% — wafer-thin for a credit book.
🔴 Acima GMV turned negative year-over-year in Q1 2026 — the growth engine has stalled, by design and by demand.
🔴 ROIC of 4.6% sits below any reasonable cost of capital — the business is not, at present, earning its keep.
🔴 Open multi-state AG / legal liabilities on legacy practices; subprime regulatory risk (CFPB posture is fluid).
🔴 Heavy, rapid C-suite turnover (new CEO, CFO, CGO, CTO inside 12 months) — can signal a reset, can also signal instability.
🟢 Free cash flow is real and robust (TTM $333M) at ~5x price-to-FCF — genuinely cheap on cash.
🟢 Deleveraging is on track and credible (2.9x → 2.6x, heading to 2x), aided by a ~$150M cash-tax tailwind from new tax policy.
🟢 Charge-offs recovered sharply in Q1 2026 (Acima −130 bps sequentially); the credit fix appears to be working.
🟢 Insider conviction is genuine: 11 open-market buys vs 2 sells — real money, not grants.
🟢 Brigit is growing ~40% and is a structurally better (subscription, asset-light) business than the lease book.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The vocabulary migrated from "growth" to "transformation" and "AI."** When a subprime lease company starts leading every call with "data, advanced analytics and AI" rather than GMV and store economics, it is repositioning the story away from a stalling core.
- **"Trade-down" went from a promise to a hope.** In Q1 2025 it was a guaranteed tailwind ("if anything, it's positive"); by Q3 2025 the same consumer was a source of "demand pressure" and "elevated losses." The thesis quietly flipped.
- **The new CFO is from goeasy** — a Canadian non-prime lender. The hire signals the board sees Upbound's future as a *disciplined credit underwriter*, not a retail-growth story.
- **The "exclusive checkout button" was walked back under questioning** (Q1 2026): management implied exclusivity, then clarified it is only the checkout button, "not exclusively… the sole rent-to-own provider." A small but telling oversell.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is a company mid-transition — from a growth-led rent-to-own/fintech story to a disciplined, deleveraging subprime credit operator betting that digital/AI initiatives compound on the far side of a credit cycle. The capital-allocation plan is coherent and conservative: cash goes to debt paydown and a maintained dividend, with M&A explicitly on the back burner ("our mode right now… is probably going to be on the conservative side").

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is optically very cheap (≈5x free cash flow, several value models showing 50–90% margins of safety) but the cheapness sits on a **low-quality, cyclically-pressured earnings base** — ROIC 4.6%, net margin 1.6%, EPS down 43%, and a growth engine (Acima) that just turned negative. The question is whether you are buying a fear-priced cash machine near the bottom of a credit cycle, or a value trap whose returns never recover above their cost of capital. There is no hard catalyst forcing the gap to close — only self-help (deleveraging plus a hoped-for second-half-2026 growth rebound).

**Moat:** Narrow. The real edge is Acima's merchant-integration network (35,000+ locations, switching costs for embedded retailers) plus proprietary subprime underwriting data. But the returns evidence — ROIC 4.6%, gross margin 34.5% and explicitly "contracting," net margin 1.6% — describes a thin, eroding franchise, not a durable one. A genuine moat throws off returns above its cost of capital; this does not, right now.

**Secular threat:** Material. Brigit's small-dollar-liquidity niche is being crowded by fintech entrants (management conceded competitors are copying it), and the broader payments/fintech disintermediation wave (buy-now-pay-later, embedded lending) competes directly with Acima's lease-to-own proposition. This is not an imminent terminal threat — durable goods for thin-file consumers is a real, persistent need — but pricing power is structurally capped.

# Upbound Group (UPBD) — Forensic Dossier

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from six consecutive earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

Upbound Group is the renamed parent of Rent-A-Center. It runs three businesses aimed at consumers who sit outside the traditional credit system: Rent-A-Center (the legacy rent-to-own store chain), Acima (a virtual lease-to-own platform embedded at the checkout of roughly 35,000-plus merchant locations), and Brigit (a subscription financial-wellness and small-dollar-liquidity app, acquired January 2025). This is, at its core, a subprime consumer-credit business dressed in fintech language.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has shifted meaningfully across these six quarters, and not entirely by choice.

**The opening note (Q1 2025) was triumphant and valedictory.** Mitch Fadel, on his "30th and final earnings call," framed Upbound as "stronger today than it's ever been," with Acima "on a tear since late 2023" booking record revenue while *improving* charge-offs. The pitch was a virtuous flywheel: trade-down demand (shoppers stepping down from prime credit) feeding Acima, a fast-growing Brigit, and a Rent-A-Center deliberately shrunk for quality.

**By mid-2025 the story tightened around discipline.** New CEO Fahmi Karam (promoted from CFO in June 2025) leaned on "protecting our balance sheet with prudent risk management" and deleveraging toward "2x leverage towards the end of next year." Growth was still the headline, but the supporting beam was credit caution.

**Q3 2025 was the crack in the narrative.** Karam had to "address the lower margin and higher loss performance at Acima" — a cohort of Q2 leases "with elevated early defaults, mainly to new customers in our e-commerce channels." The flywheel claim quietly inverted: trade-down was now a hoped-for offset to a deteriorating consumer, not a guaranteed tailwind. Management pivoted to "maybe… we will be overtightened" — choosing lower growth to defend losses.

**Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 completed the pivot to a self-help, "transformation" story.** The language is now dominated by deleveraging (2.9x → 2.6x), "data, advanced analytics and AI," and a parade of new C-suite hires (CFO Hal Khouri ex-goeasy, a Chief Growth Officer, a Chief Technology Officer). Acima GMV (gross merchandise value, the dollar value of goods leased) actually *fell year-over-year* in Q1 2026 — the first decline in the window — as tightening bit. The growth driver that powered the 2025 story has been deliberately throttled.

**Net:** the arc moved from "best-ever growth company" to "disciplined operator deleveraging through a choppy subprime cycle, hoping the AI/digital initiatives compound later." Growth was the headline in Q1 2025; balance-sheet repair is the headline now.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Acima has been on a tear… highest ever quarterly revenue" (Q1 2025); GMV +9% → +16% → +11% across 2025 | Consolidated revenue +8.7% YoY to $4.70B (FY2025); TTM revenue ~$4.5–4.7B. Real, but driven by Acima + ~two-thirds of a year of Brigit, not the whole company | **Matches — partially.** Acima growth was real; consolidated growth is more pedestrian and has now reversed, with Acima GMV turning negative in Q1 2026 |
| "Stronger today than it's ever been" (Q1 2025) | Net income $73M (FY2025) vs $123M (FY2024) — down ~41%; EPS $1.25 vs $2.21, **−43% YoY**; ROIC just 4.6% | **Diverges sharply.** Earnings nearly halved in the very year management called the company its strongest ever |
| Charge-offs improving / "within target range" | Acima charge-offs spiked to ~10% by Q4 2025 before recovering to ~8.8% in Q1 2026; net margin a razor-thin 1.6% | **Mixed.** The Q3-Q4 2025 deterioration was real and initially downplayed; the Q1 2026 recovery is genuine but recent |
| Deleveraging toward 2x | Net debt $1.63B (balance sheet, Mar 2026); leverage ~2.6x, down from 2.9x at year-end 2025 | **Matches.** The most credible part of the story — cash generation is real |
| Free cash flow strength ("nearly 4x larger" Q1 2025) | TTM FCF $333M; price-to-FCF ~5x; FY FCF 3-yr CAGR −16.3% (lumpy) | **Matches on level, not trend.** Current FCF is robust and cheap; the multi-year trend is choppy, not compounding |

The forensic tension is plain: management's prose ran hottest (Q1 2025 "best ever") in the exact year EPS fell 43% and net margin collapsed to 1.6%. The numbers say "cheap, cash-generative, but low-quality and cyclically pressured," not "best-ever."

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Declining, then stabilizing defensively.**

- **Q1 2025 (Rising/peak):** "stronger than it's ever been," "on a tear," offensive, growth-forward.
- **Q2 2025 (Stable):** "discipline in protecting our balance sheet" — first real defensive tilt; growth still claimed.
- **Q3 2025 (Declining):** forced to "address the lower margin and higher loss performance," "maybe… we will be overtightened" — clearly on the back foot.
- **Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 (Defensive-stable):** heavy reliance on "transformation," "data… AI," and leadership additions. The vocabulary shifted decisively from offense (growth, share gains) to defense (efficiency, cost optimization, prudence, "challenging operating environment"). Guidance is reaffirmed, not raised.

The shift from "trade-down is a tailwind" to "the macro is… pressuring our consumers' collective confidence" (Q3 2025) is the clearest tell.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-to-High on hitting numbers, with a sandbagging caveat.** The screener shows a 7-for-7 quarterly earnings-beat rate, and management consistently "exceeded the midpoint or high end" of guided ranges (Q1, Q2 2025). That is a real, repeatable pattern — and it cuts both ways: a 100% beat rate over seven quarters suggests deliberately conservative guideposts, so beats should be treated as expected rather than as upside surprises.

The one credibility ding: Acima's Q2-Q3 2025 loss spike was *not* foreshadowed in the Q1 2025 confidence and required mid-year mitigation. They caught it and fixed it (Q1 2026 charge-offs improved 130 bps sequentially), but they did not see it coming early. Reliability on the controllable (cost, deleveraging, guidance ranges) is High; foresight on credit vintages is Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Credit quality at Acima** — the dominant recurring question (Kyle Joseph, Bobby Griffin, Hoang Nguyen, multiple quarters). The "we're conservative / overtightened" answer was tested and partially vindicated, but the Q2-Q3 vintage problem proves analysts were right to push.
- **Legal accruals** — John Rowan (Q2 2025) pressed on a $32M accrual tied to a multi-state attorneys-general matter and the McBurnie case (a legacy Acceptance Now liability). Management framed settlements as "progress," but this is an open, multi-year overhang on a subprime lender.
- **The path back to growth in 2026** — analysts repeatedly asked whether GMV reacceleration depends on credit loosening. Management leaned on merchant-count additions and a new furniture-checkout deal, not on the consumer healing — an admission the cycle is a headwind they cannot control.
- **Brigit competition** — analysts flagged competitors "jumping along and developing or acquiring similar products." The differentiation answer was thin.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 EPS fell 43% in FY2025 (the year management called it "best ever"); net margin is just 1.6% — wafer-thin for a credit book.
🔴 Acima GMV turned negative year-over-year in Q1 2026 — the growth engine has stalled, by design and by demand.
🔴 ROIC of 4.6% sits below any reasonable cost of capital — the business is not, at present, earning its keep.
🔴 Open multi-state AG / legal liabilities on legacy practices; subprime regulatory risk (CFPB posture is fluid).
🔴 Heavy, rapid C-suite turnover (new CEO, CFO, CGO, CTO inside 12 months) — can signal a reset, can also signal instability.
🟢 Free cash flow is real and robust (TTM $333M) at ~5x price-to-FCF — genuinely cheap on cash.
🟢 Deleveraging is on track and credible (2.9x → 2.6x, heading to 2x), aided by a ~$150M cash-tax tailwind from new tax policy.
🟢 Charge-offs recovered sharply in Q1 2026 (Acima −130 bps sequentially); the credit fix appears to be working.
🟢 Insider conviction is genuine: 11 open-market buys vs 2 sells — real money, not grants.
🟢 Brigit is growing ~40% and is a structurally better (subscription, asset-light) business than the lease book.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The vocabulary migrated from "growth" to "transformation" and "AI."** When a subprime lease company starts leading every call with "data, advanced analytics and AI" rather than GMV and store economics, it is repositioning the story away from a stalling core.
- **"Trade-down" went from a promise to a hope.** In Q1 2025 it was a guaranteed tailwind ("if anything, it's positive"); by Q3 2025 the same consumer was a source of "demand pressure" and "elevated losses." The thesis quietly flipped.
- **The new CFO is from goeasy** — a Canadian non-prime lender. The hire signals the board sees Upbound's future as a *disciplined credit underwriter*, not a retail-growth story.
- **The "exclusive checkout button" was walked back under questioning** (Q1 2026): management implied exclusivity, then clarified it is only the checkout button, "not exclusively… the sole rent-to-own provider." A small but telling oversell.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is a company mid-transition — from a growth-led rent-to-own/fintech story to a disciplined, deleveraging subprime credit operator betting that digital/AI initiatives compound on the far side of a credit cycle. The capital-allocation plan is coherent and conservative: cash goes to debt paydown and a maintained dividend, with M&A explicitly on the back burner ("our mode right now… is probably going to be on the conservative side").

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is optically very cheap (≈5x free cash flow, several value models showing 50–90% margins of safety) but the cheapness sits on a **low-quality, cyclically-pressured earnings base** — ROIC 4.6%, net margin 1.6%, EPS down 43%, and a growth engine (Acima) that just turned negative. The question is whether you are buying a fear-priced cash machine near the bottom of a credit cycle, or a value trap whose returns never recover above their cost of capital. There is no hard catalyst forcing the gap to close — only self-help (deleveraging plus a hoped-for second-half-2026 growth rebound).

**Moat:** Narrow. The real edge is Acima's merchant-integration network (35,000+ locations, switching costs for embedded retailers) plus proprietary subprime underwriting data. But the returns evidence — ROIC 4.6%, gross margin 34.5% and explicitly "contracting," net margin 1.6% — describes a thin, eroding franchise, not a durable one. A genuine moat throws off returns above its cost of capital; this does not, right now.

**Secular threat:** Material. Brigit's small-dollar-liquidity niche is being crowded by fintech entrants (management conceded competitors are copying it), and the broader payments/fintech disintermediation wave (buy-now-pay-later, embedded lending) competes directly with Acima's lease-to-own proposition. This is not an imminent terminal threat — durable goods for thin-file consumers is a real, persistent need — but pricing power is structurally capped.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE** (steady, credible execution through a self-corrected credit wobble; a transformation underway but not yet re-rating the returns).

Across the eight quarters on tape (first-quarter 2025 through first-quarter 2026), the story moved from an offensive "digital financial platform" expansion to a defensive "protect the balance sheet and the credit book" posture, then back toward cautious optimism.

- **Early 2025 (offensive):** Mitch Fadel's farewell call framed Upbound as a three-brand platform — Rent-A-Center (the legacy lease-to-own stores), Acima (virtual, merchant-embedded lease-to-own), and the newly acquired Brigit (subscription financial-wellness and cash-advance app). The pitch: unify the consumer data across all three to cross-sell an underserved, non-prime customer. Acima was "on a tear," booking record revenue with falling charge-offs.
- **Mid-to-late 2025 (defensive pivot):** Fahmi Karam took over as chief executive. By the third quarter he was pre-emptively addressing "lower margin and higher loss performance at Acima" — second-quarter lease vintages showed elevated early defaults among new e-commerce customers. Management tightened underwriting hard (approval rates cut ~200 basis points year-to-date) and accepted that this would suppress gross merchandise volume (GMV) growth. The language shifted from "growth algorithm" to "protecting the portfolio."
- **Early 2026 (stabilize-and-rebuild):** First-quarter 2026 confirmed the repair — Acima charge-offs improved ~130 basis points sequentially to ~8.8%. But GMV came in below plan and below the prior-year quarter. Management guided to a back-half-2026 recovery, hinging on merchant additions (including new exclusive checkout rights at "the largest e-commerce furniture retailer in the country") rather than looser credit.
- **Now (second-quarter 2026, 2026-07-30):** Results met estimates but the full-year revenue outlook was trimmed — the "more cautious sales view" the wire services flagged. The narrative is intact but the top-line recovery keeps sliding to the right.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director) — **STABLE**

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the cheapness is sector-wide, not name-specific.** The direct rent-to-own peer (Aaron's) trades at a similarly depressed low-single-digit cash-flow multiple; the whole subprime lease-to-own cohort has been re-rated down on secular-volume and consumer-credit fears. So the discount is largely shared-factor beta, and the re-rating waits on the sector — and on Acima's GMV actually inflecting — not on a company-specific unlock.

**Moat:** intangible/data plus a merchant-network switching cost at Acima (35,000+ locations, API-embedded checkout) — real but **narrow**; Rent-A-Center's store moat is a fading regional-inertia advantage. Returns are middling, not clearly rising, so the moat is narrow and roughly **stable**, not widening.

**Secular threat:** **manageable, not terminal.** Buy-now-pay-later and fintech lending compete for the same durable-goods checkout, but Acima *is* the fintech-enabled expression (virtual lease card, direct-to-consumer marketplace up 100%+), and the underserved non-prime lease-to-own niche persists through cycles. The pressure is cyclical-consumer and channel-mix, not a melting terminal base. Cheapness here is closer to a fear-print than a value trap — but a fear-print the whole sector shares.
